sections.title: The Prohibitions of Sorcery
sections.html:
God commanded Israel not to engage in any kind of sorcery, as it is stated (Devarim 18:9-15): "When you come into the land that the Lord your God is giving you, you shall not learn to do according to the abominations of those nations. There shall not be found among you one who passes his son or his daughter through the fire, one who practises divination, a soothsayer, an augur or a sorcerer, or a charmer, or one who consults a ghost or a familiar spirit, or one who inquires of the dead. For whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord, and because of these abominations the Lord your God is driving them out before you. You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God. For these nations that you are dispossessing listen to soothsayers and diviners, but as for you, the Lord your God has not permitted you to do so. A prophet from your midst, from your brothers, like me, will the Lord your God raise up for you; to him you shall listen." Sorcerers have two main aims: a) to bring about changes in reality, such as casting a curse on a person in order to cause his death or to make him poor; b) to know hidden things and the future. All activities in these matters are included under the name sorcery (kishuf), and some of them also have a specific name (Ramban, Devarim 18:9-12; Tur 179:16).

In general, the prohibitions of sorcery rest on the pagan conception, according to which God, the God of gods, does not govern His world; rather, the world is run by various separate forces. Those who sin with idolatry relate to the various forces as idols and bow down to them so that they will help them, whereas those who sin with sorcery do not bow down to idols but rather try to manipulate the idols, or spiritual forces lower than them, in order to bring about changes in reality or to know hidden things, as will be explained below (sections 6-8).

There are two aspects to the prohibition. The first is that one may not use forces of impurity (tum'a) in order to break through the boundaries of nature. The second is that one must conduct oneself wholeheartedly with God and accept His guidance with faith that everything is for the good. And although a person longs to know the future, he is commanded to restrain himself and wait until things actually happen, and not to resort to crooked ways in order to divine the future. And if trouble comes upon him, he should not try to escape it by unnatural means, but should rather contend with it according to God's guidance in the Torah and within the framework of the laws of nature that the Creator established, and through this he will be refined, will rise and will truly advance. This also includes praying to God, for prayer is one of the ways God has given man to draw close to Him and to repair himself, and through this God will bless him. Even in order to advance good aims it is forbidden to use sorcery, because Israel must add goodness and blessing to the world by way of the Torah, within the framework of the laws of nature; and even if this way is long, the repair (tikkun) it brings is deep and fundamental, and it advances us stage after stage toward the repair of man and the world.

Sorcery is performed by reciting incantations and by various actions, such as combining certain substances and burning them as incense. For three kinds of sorcery one is liable to the severe death penalty of stoning, and they are: the sorcerer (mekhashef), as it is stated (Shemot 22:17): "You shall not let a sorceress live"; and the ba'al ov and the yidde'oni (necromancers), as it is stated (Vayikra 20:27): "A man or a woman in whom there is a ghost or a familiar spirit shall surely be put to death; they shall stone them with stones; their blood is upon them." The other kinds of sorcery are forbidden by a negative commandment, and one who sins with them before witnesses who warned him is liable to lashes (see above 3:2).

sections.title: The Exodus from Egypt and the Subjugation of the Sorcerers of Egypt
sections.html:
At the Exodus from Egypt, together with Israel's going out from servitude to freedom, faith too, which had been enslaved to pagan conceptions and to the deeds of sorcerers, went out from darkness to light. For this is the destiny of the people of Israel: to contend with the gravest darkness, and through the course of its history to reveal the light of pure faith and to bring redemption to the world, as it is stated (Yeshayahu 43:21): "This people I formed for Myself; they shall recount My praise." Therefore Israel was enslaved specifically in Egypt, where the most crudely material pagan belief prevailed (see Maharal, Gevurot Hashem ch. 4). And there were the greatest sorcerers, as the Sages said (Kiddushin 49b): "Ten kabs of sorcery came down to the world; Egypt took nine, and the whole rest of the world one."

And although God could have taken Israel out in a single day, He hardened Pharaoh's heart so that he would refuse to send them out, so that it would be necessary to strike Egypt with ten plagues, and in this way the whole world would know that God rules over all the forces in the world, and that even the idols of Egypt and their sorcerers cannot stand against Him. As it is stated (Shemot 7:4-5): "But Pharaoh will not listen to you, and I will lay My hand upon Egypt and bring out My hosts – My people the children of Israel – from the land of Egypt with great judgments. And Egypt shall know that I am the Lord, when I stretch out My hand over Egypt and bring out the children of Israel from among them" (Derashot Ha-Ran 3; Abarbanel, Shemot 4:10).

From the very beginning, when Moshe and Aharon came on God's mission to demand that Pharaoh send Israel out, Pharaoh drew strength from his idols and his sorcerers and said: "Who is the Lord, that I should listen to His voice to send Israel out? I do not know the Lord, and moreover I will not send Israel out" (Shemot 5:2). Therefore God commanded Moshe and Aharon (Shemot 7:9-13): "When Pharaoh speaks to you, saying, 'Show a wonder for yourselves,' you shall say to Aharon, 'Take your staff and cast it down before Pharaoh; let it become a serpent.' And Moshe and Aharon came to Pharaoh and did so, as the Lord had commanded; and Aharon cast down his staff before Pharaoh and before his servants, and it became a serpent. Then Pharaoh too called for the wise men and the sorcerers, and they too, the magicians of Egypt, did likewise with their secret arts; each man cast down his staff, and they became serpents." At that moment the wise men of Egypt wondered at Moshe and Aharon for daring to compete with them in sorcery, since the sorcerers of Egypt were the greatest in the world (see Menaḥot 85a).

Afterward God commanded Moshe to strike Egypt with blood, and the magicians also showed that with their sorcery they could turn water into blood, as it is stated (ibid. 7:15-22): "Thus says the Lord: By this you shall know that I am the Lord: behold, I will strike with the staff that is in my hand upon the water that is in the Nile, and it shall be turned to blood… And he (Aharon) raised the staff and struck the water that was in the Nile before the eyes of Pharaoh and before the eyes of his servants, and all the water that was in the Nile was turned to blood… And the magicians of Egypt did likewise with their secret arts, and Pharaoh's heart was hardened and he did not listen to them, as the Lord had spoken." In the plague of frogs as well the sorcerers stood against God, as it is stated (ibid. 8:2-3): "And Aharon stretched out his hand over the waters of Egypt, and the frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt. And the magicians did likewise with their secret arts, and brought up frogs upon the land of Egypt."

They also tried with the plague of lice, as it is stated (ibid. 8:13-14): "And Aharon stretched out his hand with his staff and struck the dust of the earth, and there were lice on man and on beast; all the dust of the earth became lice throughout the land of Egypt. And the magicians did likewise with their secret arts to bring forth lice, but they could not; and there were lice on man and on beast." Then the magicians understood that the plagues were not brought about by sorcery but came from God: "And the magicians said to Pharaoh: It is the finger of God" (ibid. 15; Rashi).

Pharaoh continued to harden his heart, and the plagues with which God struck Egypt grew ever stronger, until many of the sorcerers recognised the great power of God. The Sages said (Zohar II 191a) that some of them joined Israel, as it is stated (Shemot 12:38): "And a mixed multitude also went up with them." However, later, when Moshe Rabbeinu delayed in coming down from Mount Sinai, there were sorcerers there who by their sorcery caused the gold that Aharon melted down to become the golden calf, and it was they who led Israel to sin by saying: "These are your gods, O Israel, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt" (Shemot 32:4 and Rashi; see Peninei Halakha, Giyur 3:1).

sections.title: The Laws of Sorcery
sections.html:
The Sages said (Sanhedrin 67b): there are three rulings regarding sorcery and acts resembling sorcery: a) When the sorcerer changes things in the world, he is liable to death by stoning. b) When he appears to change things but has not really changed them, although he transgresses a Torah prohibition, he is not liable to death. As an example of this, they told of someone who cut up a camel into pieces with his sword, then rang a bell, and the camel got up and stood on its feet. Rabbi Ḥiyya wanted to know whether, after it stood up, any remnants of blood and dung were left, and when they answered him that none were left, he said that this was a matter of a person deceiving the eyes (an illusionist) and not a sorcerer. c) When the change in reality is brought about through Sefer Yetzira, it is permitted (below, 20:3-4, it will be explained that it is not desirable to do so).1

It is not proper to engage in studying matters of sorcery, but in order to understand the commandments of the Torah that prohibited sorcery, it is permitted, and even a mitzva, for Torah scholars to study the practices of sorcery. As it is stated (Devarim 18:9): "You shall not learn to do according to the abominations of those nations," and the Sages expounded (Sanhedrin 68a): "To do you may not learn, but you may learn in order to understand and to teach." Moreover, the Sages said (Sanhedrin 17a): "Only men of stature, men of wisdom… and masters of sorcery are seated on the Sanhedrin," that is, people well versed in the ways of sorcery, so that they could rule on the laws concerning them (Rambam, Hilkhot Sanhedrin 2:1). And also so "that if the defendant is a sorcerer and fire has no power over him, they will perform sorcery and put him to death by whatever death they can" (Rashi, Menaḥot 65a). And also so that they could distinguish between a true prophet and one who performs signs by sorcery (see Rav Hai Gaon, Sha'arei Teshuva 14). It follows that they needed to know how sorcery is actually performed.

Even after the destruction of the Temple, when the courts no longer judged these cases, the great sages are commanded, as part of the mitzva of Torah study, to study the ways of sorcery. As is related (Sanhedrin 68a) of Rabbi Eliezer and his disciple Rabbi Akiva, who were walking on the road: Rabbi Akiva asked Rabbi Eliezer to teach him the sorcerers' ways of planting cucumbers. Rabbi Eliezer said one incantation, and the whole field filled with cucumbers. Rabbi Akiva asked him to teach him the ways of uprooting them. Rabbi Eliezer said another incantation, and they all gathered into one place. It follows that even when there is no practical need for it, it is a mitzva for the great sages to study the ways of sorcery, in order to understand the depth of the Torah's guidance (Ḥatam Sofer, YD 128; Darkhei Teshuva 141:30; Rav Kook, Shemona Kevatzim 2:7).2

sections.title: Those Who Hold That Sorcery Is Falsehood
sections.html:
The Rishonim disagreed over whether sorcerers truly succeed in acting through their sorcery and in foreseeing the future. Some hold that all their deeds are falsehood, as the Rambam wrote (Hilkhot Avoda Zara 11:16): "And all these things are words of falsehood and deceit, and they are what the ancient idolaters used to mislead the nations of the lands so that they would follow them. And it is not fitting for Israel, who are exceedingly wise, to be drawn after these vanities, nor to imagine that there is any benefit in them. As it is stated: 'For there is no augury in Yaakov, nor divination in Israel,' and it is stated: 'For these nations that you are dispossessing listen to soothsayers and diviners, but as for you, the Lord your God has not permitted you to do so.' Whoever believes in these things and the like, and thinks in his heart that they are true and matters of wisdom but the Torah forbade them, is nothing but one of the fools and those lacking understanding… But the wise and those of sound understanding will know with clear proofs that all these things that the Torah forbade are not matters of wisdom but emptiness and vanity, after which those lacking understanding were drawn and for whose sake they abandoned all the paths of truth. And for this reason the Torah said, when it warned against all these vanities: 'You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God.'" According to those who hold this view, the sorcery for which one is liable to stoning is sorcery by which many people believe the sorcerer succeeded in bringing about real changes in the world, but in practice the sorcery brought about no change at all.

However, even according to those who hold that sorcerers have no real power, the very fact that people believe they have supernatural powers causes the sorcerers to have a psychological influence over them, by virtue of which it is even possible that they will be healed or fall ill, grow stronger or weaker. In addition, there are psychological depths in the subconscious that talented sorcerers can understand and through which they can influence people.

And although from the words of the Sages in many places it appears that they related to sorcery as something real, the Rambam and those who hold like him explain that these words of the Sages are a parable or a secret that is not to be understood literally. And some say that the Rambam too agrees that sorcerers sometimes succeeded in changing things through their sorcery, but in the end they prove false and those who rely on them come to grief, and therefore they are falsehood.3

sections.title: In the View of Many, Sorcery Has Power
sections.html:
In the view of most of the sages of Israel, sorcerers have the power to change things and to know hidden things, but their power is not constant, and very often they err and fail. As the Ramban wrote (Devarim 18:9): "And many make a show of piety regarding auguries, saying that there is no truth in them at all, for who will tell the raven and the crane what will be. But we cannot deny things that become known before the eyes of onlookers. And our Rabbis too acknowledge them…." But in contrast to the sorcerers, who very often err and mislead, God gave us true prophets. As the Sages said (Sifrei there): "Lest you say: They have something to inquire of, and I have nothing! Therefore the verse says: 'But as for you, the Lord your God has not permitted you to do so'"; rather, He gave you true prophets who continue the guidance of the Torah (see above 16:3).

However, even in their view, since these are hidden forces that are difficult to measure, there are many liars in this field. Some of them deceive themselves into thinking that they have spiritual powers; some know that they have no powers and deceive people into thinking that they do; and some had powers in the past and lost them over time, yet continue to deceive themselves and others that they still have powers. Nevertheless, in their view it cannot be denied that there are people with special spiritual abilities to see and sense beyond the ordinary, and when they connect to forces of impurity through sorcery, they are able to intensify their power to know the future, and sometimes also to bring things about.4

sections.title: Sorcery and Its Impurity: An Explanation of Concepts
sections.html:
In order to understand the explanations of the masters of the hidden wisdom regarding the activity of sorcerers with the help of the forces of impurity, seemingly against the will of God, several concepts must be explained. 'Impurity' (tum'a) is opacity, concealment and disconnection. That is, the impure becomes sealed off and hidden from the supernal divine light, and thereby becomes disconnected from the source of its life. Therefore impurity is bound up with death, and the dead is the ultimate source of impurity (avi avot ha-tum'a), for his body has been sealed off from the divine light that gives it life. By contrast, 'purity' (tahara) carries the sense of an opening through which a connection is made to the divine source of life.

Above this world there exist 'upper worlds', that is, higher spiritual levels. In each world, all the creatures and values known to us from this world find spiritual expression according to the level of that world. In the order of creation, God first created the upper world, in which the divine light shines more strongly, and therefore ideas appear in it more clearly and deeply. Afterwards He gradually created world after world, down to this world, and through the divine light God bestows life on all the worlds, down to this world. The lower the world, the weaker the divine light that reaches it, down to the physical world, in which the divine light is hidden within all the creatures, and thereby the world exists as a physical world in which the influence of the divine light is not revealed, and consequently human beings have an awareness of independent existence and free choice. A further meaning: the more the divine light descends through the worlds and becomes corporeal, the weaker its light becomes and the more deficiencies it has, because of which more severe crises took place. These deficiencies and crises are the evil that God created in the world.

The worlds through which the divine light descends to this world are called worlds of holiness. All the good traits, such as kindness and truth, appear in these worlds in a higher form, and through them life is added to the world. Since created beings cannot be perfect, opposite every world of holiness there is a world of impurity, composed of all the flaws, deficiencies, illusions, errors, disappointments and crises ('the breaking of the vessels', shevirat ha-kelim) of the corresponding world of holiness. The worlds of impurity are the source of all the bad traits that we encounter in this world, such as treachery, falsehood, greed, lust, the urge to win and the pursuit of honour. That is, out of the deficiencies and crises in the worlds of impurity arises despair of connecting to God, the source of life, and of drawing blessing into the world; and consequently, until everything breaks and dies, all that is left for a person is to be dragged after the bad traits and to satisfy his desires as far as he can: "Eat and drink, for tomorrow we die" (Yeshayahu 22:13).

Through the creation of evil, God granted man the power to choose between good and evil. If he chooses good, he will connect to the spiritual roots of the good in the worlds of holiness and will add goodness and blessing to the world. And if he chooses evil, he will connect to the bad traits in the worlds of impurity, will diminish the light and life flowing into this world, and will cause death and destruction. In this way God granted man the ability to merit the divine good through his own choice, and thereby his happiness will be increased by all the good he acquired by virtue of his choice. In addition, evil has a very important role: to criticise the good; for since the good is limited, it must be criticised so that it may be refined and perfected (see above 1:17).

The righteous cleave to God, the source of life, and through the Torah, the mitzvot and good deeds they add life to all the worlds, down to this world. And the pure righteous even add illumination to the broken worlds, in order to heal and repair their breaks, and to light a path for sinners to return in repentance and to turn their sins from wilful transgressions into merits. Death too is not final for the righteous, for their souls merit the life of the World to Come. Therefore even after their death they are called living (Berakhot 18a).

But the wicked do not believe that it is possible to connect to God, the source of life, and to repair the breaks, and by means of the bad traits they try to satisfy their desires, and thereby they render themselves and those around them impure, that is, they disconnect them from the root of life. Therefore even in their lifetimes the wicked are called dead (Berakhot 18b). Out of that same outlook of despair, sorcerers act through the forces of impurity to block the abundance that descends from the spiritual worlds into this world or to divert it for their own needs. Their activity is carried out through various techniques, such as those explained in the following sections.5

sections.title: The Power of Letters and Speech
sections.html:
The main activity of sorcerers is through incantations based on letters and speech. In order to understand their power, it must first be noted that in 'Sefer Yetzira', which is attributed to Avraham Avinu, it is explained that at first God created the ten sefirot, that is, ten aspects of the manifestation of God's governance in the world, and the twenty-two letters, and through them He created the world. Each of the sefirot and letters has its own particular essence, and from their primal combination God formed His holy names, through which He was revealed to the world. On the basis of the holy names and further letters He created the roots of the elements, which afterwards devolved to become physical elements, such as atoms and states of matter. Through further joining and combining of the letters in various forms, God formed the roots of all creatures, in their kinds and particulars. In this way the letters and words progressively became corporeal from world to world, down to the creatures in this world. It follows that God created the world through letters and speech. He said "'Let there be light' – and there was light" (Bereshit 1:3), and as long as the divine utterance "Let there be light" continues, the light continues to exist. And so with all creatures. In the world above this world, the letters and words at the roots of created beings are called angels (mal'akhim), that is, messengers who uphold the laws that God engraved in the letters, and through them life flows to those beneath them. For example, every species of plant or animal has an angel through which it exists. The angel is also called a 'mazal', through which life flows (nozlim) to that plant.

It follows that every created being has an inner spiritual root in the world above it, and so on, world above world, and God, may He be blessed, bestows life through the letters and names on all the worlds. At the conclusion of the order of creation, God created man in the 'image of God', that is, in such a way that he too can speak and act in the world and change it for good or for bad. Through speech he can learn and teach how to walk in God's ways and cooperate with his fellows to add goodness and blessing to the world; or, the opposite, arouse them to pursue false desires wickedly. The Torah that God gave to Israel is the complete guidance on how to connect to God and walk in His ways, for the Torah is the revelation of God's name in the world, and the divine plan for the creation of the world and its repair is hidden within it. Therefore, through studying Torah and fulfilling the mitzvot, Israel draws blessing into the world, elevates it and repairs it.

There is also a superficial and peripheral way of influencing the world, called 'practical Kabbala' (kabbala ma'asit); that is, a person who knows the secret of the names and letters in Sefer Yetzira can create things in the world through holy names and combinations of letters. And since he does so in accordance with the rules by which the world was created, there is no prohibition in his deeds. However, there are problems and dangers in this way, as will be explained below (20:1-4).

In contrast to this, sorcerers can, through words of incantation, connect to the roots of evil in the worlds of impurity, and through them change the letters and words through which the abundance flows into the world, and thus cause harm to whomever they wish to curse. Since they do this not in accordance with the divine purpose, they spoil the orderly flow of good influence descending from above, as the Sages said (Sanhedrin 67b): "Why are they called kishafim (sorcery)? Because they contradict (makhḥishim) the heavenly household (pamalya shel ma'ala)" (Derekh Hashem part 3, 2:7-9).6

sections.title: Sorcery and Its Development Through Strengthening in Wickedness
sections.html:
God granted man a talent for connecting to upper worlds, that is, to higher levels, above this world and its laws. If he does so in holiness, he will understand the Torah and its secrets, and will add goodness and blessing to the world. On the other hand, if he does so in impurity, he will be able to understand the roots of evil and its ways of operating, and will be able to devise incantations capable of acting to satisfy his desires. For "God has made the one opposite the other." Just as He created the good orders of the world, which are the foundation of the good traits, such as kindness and truth, righteousness and justice, all of which are included in the ten sefirot of each world; so He created the forces of destruction, which are the foundation of the bad traits, such as lust, envy and honour, and these too are included in the ten impure sefirot of each world of impurity. Just as in holiness one can, through prayers to God and the performance of mitzvot, draw blessing into the world and merit the life of the World to Come, so correspondingly in impurity one can, through incantations and acts of sorcery, block the abundance of life of whomever one wishes to curse. Thus, for the sake of attaining his desire, he will lose true and eternal life. The more the sorcerers became addicted to their evil inclination, the more powerful the sorcery they could devise and the greater the force with which they could activate it, and the more they were punished in Gehinnom. As the Sages said (Avot 5:19) of the wicked sorcerer Bilam, that in him and his disciples were these three things: 'an evil eye' – envious of others; 'a haughty spirit' – arrogant; and 'a broad appetite' (nefesh reḥava) – lustful. And their end: they "inherit Gehinnom and go down to the pit of destruction." And the Sages also said (Avot 4:21): "Envy, desire and honour remove a person from the world."

As stated, sorcery is mainly performed by incantation, that is, speech using the letters through which life flows to the things one wishes to influence. In order to strengthen the sorcery, sorcerers use various substances connected to the change they wish to bring about. This is based on the recognition that all the components of the world are connected to one another and influence one another, and when the sorcerer recites an incantation over a certain substance against a certain person, he can block or change the abundance flowing to him. Since their main aim is to do evil, they made much use of poisonous substances, or of hair and nails, which are things that grew from the body, were cut off from it and died. And if they succeeded in taking hair or nails from the body of the person they wished to curse, they could strengthen even more the sorcery they wished to cast upon him.7

sections.title: Sorcery Against the Righteous
sections.html:
The way of the great sorcerers was that, out of an outlook of despair of the good and of life, they knew how to expose the moral weak point of the person they wished to curse, and through this they would bring accusation against him; and at the moment when wrath was aroused against him on high, they would curse him, and by virtue of the justice in the accusation their curse would take effect. Therefore, in principle, sorcery can harm even good and righteous people, for since the sin of Adam, the evil inclination has entered all human beings, and there is no righteous person on earth who has no weak point through which sorcerers can try to harm him. And just as if a wicked person strikes a righteous person a mortal blow, the righteous person will die, so if the sorcerer succeeds in bringing accusation against the righteous person and whispering a sorcerer's incantation against him, he will disrupt his channels of abundance and harm him, and may even cause his death. And so the Sages said (Berakhot 7a) that the wicked Bilam intended to bring accusation against Israel, and then, at the moment wrath would be aroused against them, to curse them with a curse of annihilation. But in order to save Israel, throughout all those days God was not angry with Israel, and Bilam could not curse them, as he said (Bamidbar 23:8): "How shall I curse whom God has not cursed, and how shall I denounce whom the Lord has not denounced?"

The more a person rises in the levels of righteousness, the more the sorcerers' power to harm him diminishes. For just as there are levels in holiness, so correspondingly there are levels in impurity, and only if the sorcerer succeeds in connecting to a higher level of impurity than the righteous person's corresponding level in holiness can he harm him. It is related (Sanhedrin 67b) of a sorceress who tried to take dust from under the feet of Rabbi Ḥanina in order to cast a powerful spell on him. Rabbi Ḥanina said to her: I do not fear this, "for the Lord is God; there is none besides Him" (Devarim 4:35). The intent is not that he relied on a miracle that God would perform for him on account of his merits, for it is not proper for a person to regard himself as so righteous that God is obliged to save him by a miracle. Rather, Rabbi Ḥanina recognised in himself that he had risen to a level above sorcery, to the level at which he was wholehearted in his faith that God governs everything, and in such a state sorcery cannot interpose between him and the divine governance and cannot harm him. And even if some harm befalls him through them, it is by individual divine providence from God and for his good.8

sections.title: The Kinds of Sorcery, and the Ḥover Ḥaver (Charmer)
sections.html:
Among the forbidden kinds of sorcery, the Torah enumerated eight types, as it is stated (Devarim 18:10-11): "one who practises divination, a soothsayer, an augur or a sorcerer, or a charmer, or one who consults a ghost or a familiar spirit, or one who inquires of the dead."

Two of them deal with the attempt to change things in reality, and their matter is explained in this chapter: a) the mekhashef (sorcerer) – this is one who whispers incantations and performs actions in order to change things in reality (as explained above, halakhot 3, 7-8); b) the ḥover ḥaver (charmer) – this is one who whispers incantations to influence animals, as explained further on in this halakha.

The rest deal with the attempt to know the future in order to help a person plan his actions. Three of them make use of the dead: a) the sho'el ov (one who consults a ghost) – he is one who performs actions in order to force the dead to rise from their graves and tell him the future (below 26:3); b) the yidde'oni – he performs actions of another kind in order to force the dead to rise from their graves and tell him the future (ibid.); c) the doresh el ha-metim (one who inquires of the dead) – he is one who performs actions so that the dead, while still in their graves, will reveal the future to him (below 26:6).

Three are not connected to the dead: a) the kosem kesamim (one who practises divination) – he is one who performs various actions in order to know the future (below 24:1); b) the me'onen (soothsayer) – this is one who calculates times – which time is good and which is bad (below 24:2); c) the menaḥesh (augur) – this is one who determines, on the basis of events that happened to a person, what will be in the future and what it is worthwhile to do (below 24:3).

Generally sorcery is meant to influence people, but there is also sorcery meant to control animals, and it is included in the prohibition of ḥover ḥaver. The prohibition is to say an incantation in order to control harmful animals and force them to join together or to fight one another. Generally this was used to prevent animals from harming a person, his property and his fields, and sometimes to set the animals upon enemies. The prohibition applies to large animals such as wolves and leopards, or small ones such as snakes, scorpions, mosquitoes and fleas, and likewise to species different from one another, such as a bee and a scorpion. One who transgresses the prohibition of ḥover ḥaver is liable to lashes (Sanhedrin 65a; Tur and SA 179:5). A further type of the prohibition of ḥover ḥaver is connected to activating demons (below 26:10).9

sections.title: Bnei Noaḥ and White Magic
sections.html:
The prohibitions of sorcery do not apply to Bnei Noaḥ. This is because only the people of Israel, which was chosen to be God's people, merited the Revelation at Mount Sinai in which faith in God's unity was revealed, and merited that prophecy rest upon its great ones, was commanded to conduct itself wholeheartedly with God and to accept His governance with a whole heart, without seeking other spiritual ways to advance itself apart from the Torah and the mitzvot. As was said to Israel in the passage in which sorcery was forbidden (Devarim 18:12-15): "For whoever does these things is an abomination to the Lord, and because of these abominations the Lord your God is driving them out before you. You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God. For these nations that you are dispossessing listen to soothsayers and diviners, but as for you, the Lord your God has not permitted you to do so. A prophet from your midst, from your brothers, like me, will the Lord your God raise up for you; to him you shall listen."

And although many of the sorcerers acted within the framework of a pagan worldview, since sorcery involves no bowing down to idols but rather an attempt to manipulate them, sorcery is not included in the idolatry forbidden to Bnei Noaḥ (above 5:1). However, it seems that when sorcery is done wickedly, in order to kill or to steal or to cause harm, it is forbidden as a branch of the prohibition of murder or as a branch of the prohibition of robbery and of [the commandment of] laws (dinim).

But when sorcery is not used to commit crimes against others, Bnei Noaḥ have no prohibition against engaging in it. Therefore Bnei Noaḥ have no prohibition against engaging in 'white magic', that is, sorcery meant to help people.10

sections.title: "You Shall Be Wholehearted"
sections.html:
After the Torah forbade all kinds of sorcery to Israel, it went on to command that we conduct ourselves wholeheartedly with God, as it is stated (Devarim 18:13): "You shall be wholehearted (tamim) with the Lord your God." Tamim means whole, without any crack or flaw. Wholehearted with God means believing in God with complete faith. Had it said only, "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord," one could have made do with the belief that God created the world and gives it life. But since it says "with the Lord your God," the intent is to believe that God governs the world in the most perfect way for every person. For the name 'Elohim' means the Master of all the forces, and 'your God' (Elohekha) means the One who governs all the forces of the world with individual providence for you (Malbim, Devarim 18:13). Therefore, if a person merits something good, he should thank God for it and strengthen himself to continue walking in His ways, studying His Torah and fulfilling His mitzvot. And if something bad happens to him, he should believe that it is for the good and is meant to improve his ways, so that he can merit the divine good, and therefore he should thank God for the bad just as he thanks Him for the good.

Included in this, the wholehearted person does not try to know the future and hidden things through the crooked ways of diviners and sorcerers, who do not cleave to truth and goodness. For a person must conduct himself in the world according to the intellect with which God has graced him. And if, according to the intellect, he has no reliable and good way of knowing what will be in the future, the implication is that it is proper for him to live with the awareness that everything is open, and when whatever happens happens, he should deal with it in faith, and through this he will merit cleaving to God and receiving His blessing. And so Rashi explained (Devarim 18:13): "'You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God' – walk with Him wholeheartedly and look forward to Him, and do not inquire into the future; rather, whatever comes upon you, accept it wholeheartedly, and then you will be with Him and His portion."

For the destiny of man is to cleave to God and walk in His ways, to study His Torah and fulfil His mitzvot, so that he may be a partner with God in revealing His light and blessing, and in repairing the world with righteousness and justice. For the realisation of this destiny he must devote all his powers, talents, property and status, as it is stated (Devarim 6:5): "And you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your might." And all the trials that pass over him come from God, in order to direct him and raise him toward his great destiny; therefore he must contend with all trials and challenges within the framework of the laws and rules that God implanted in the world, without seeking the crooked ways of sorcerers and diviners in order to escape them. This is the meaning of the mitzva "You shall be wholehearted with the Lord your God."11

Indeed, people sometimes turned to the prophets as well in order to solve personal problems, like Shaul, who asked Shmuel the prophet where the donkeys that his father had lost were. But unlike the sorcerers, whose aim is to attain the desires of this world without any meaning of faith or morality, the main destiny of the prophets was to guide the people in the ways of God, and in the course of this they also helped people in matters of the moment (above 16:2). And some of the great Rishonim further explained that the aim of the prophets in revealing the future and hidden things for the needs of this world was to save Israel from the temptation to follow sorcerers and diviners (above 16:3). And through their connection to the prophets of Israel, when they went to ask about the future in matters of the moment, they also received guidance for walking in the ways of God.12

sections.title: Wholeheartedness Leads to Wisdom and Success
sections.html:
Wholeheartedness leads to wisdom, for those who try to know hidden things and the future neglect what they can learn and know with the help of the intellect that God has granted them, and instead try to attain through sorcery something they are unable to attain fully. It turns out that even if they sometimes succeed in knowing hidden things, as a result of their negligence in developing the ability to examine reality through the intellect, they will very often make more serious mistakes. Fortune-tellers think that the wholehearted person, who does not make use of sorcerers to know hidden things, is a fool. But in truth the wholehearted person is wiser than they, for he does not try to know things beyond the grasp of his intellect, and by virtue of this he will focus all his efforts within the realm of his grasp, and will merit becoming truly wise.

Therefore it is precisely wholeheartedness that brings success, for the wholehearted person makes use of his own intellect and that of his fellows in order to plan his actions, and engages diligently in the settlement of the world. By virtue of the wholeheartedness of his faith, he is not tempted to shorten his path by making use of sorcerers and fortune-tellers of all kinds, because he accepts God's governance and knows that nature was created by God so that when he tries to build his life within its framework, he will merit true elevation. And even if he has failures, they will be for his good, for they will give him lessons that will bring him closer to true success. By contrast, those who choose to make use of various forces outside the way of nature, instead of mending their ways, working diligently and striving to develop means of improving the world in the way of nature, seek short and easy ways to grow rich and gain honour. And even if they succeed in growing rich with the help of sorcery, in the long term they will not profit, for instead of learning a lesson from troubles and being built up by the effort of engaging in the settlement of the world, they will remain with all their flaws and deficiencies, and as a result they will lose their wealth and honour and inherit sorrow and sighing.13

And so Avraham Avinu, the first of the believers, was commanded (Bereshit 17:1-2): "Walk before Me and be wholehearted. And I will set My covenant between Me and you, and I will multiply you exceedingly." That is, precisely by walking wholeheartedly, without seeking crooked ways to increase his wealth, he will merit greater blessing, for he will cleave to the ways of God and merit His blessing. And so he taught his sons and disciples, as the Sages said (Avot 5:19), that the disciples of Avraham Avinu have traits opposite to those of the disciples of the wicked Bilam (above halakha 8): they have 'a good eye', not envying their fellows but rejoicing in their lot; 'a humble spirit' – they are modest and accept God's governance with love; 'a lowly appetite' (nefesh shefala) – they do not crave what is not in their hands. By virtue of this they merit enjoyment in this world and in the World to Come, as it is stated (Mishlei 8:21): "To cause those who love Me to inherit substance, and I will fill their treasuries."

sections.title: The Diminishing of Spiritual Powers
sections.html:
Following the destruction of the First Temple, prophecy began to diminish, until at the beginning of the Second Temple period prophecy departed. In parallel, the power of attraction of idolatry also diminished, and the power of the sorcerers weakened. In that period the status of wisdom rose, and the emphasis shifted from knowing God and serving Him through prophecy and the powers of emotion and imagination, to knowing God and serving Him through the intellect and deeds. In this way we passed from the era of the prophets to the era of the Sages. In the era of the prophets, Israel absorbed the great foundations of faith and of walking in the ways of God, but in parallel the forces of impurity in idol worship and sorcery also grew stronger, until Israel could not withstand them and sinned with idolatry, forbidden sexual relations and bloodshed, and the First Temple was destroyed. Then the last of the prophets held that it was better to give up prophecy and to continue guiding the people by intensifying Torah study and establishing enactments (takkanot) to root the observance of the Torah's mitzvot in the people, such as the enactment of the prayers, the blessings and the Torah reading. In this way they laid the foundation for the 'Oral Torah', by virtue of which the people of Israel grew stronger in observing the Torah and mitzvot, and even succeeded in surviving all the years of exile. In parallel, the Sages began to institute fences around the Torah, such as the prohibition of 'muktzeh' on Shabbat. In this way they fenced Israel off from transgressing the Torah's mitzvot (see above 16:18).

This process took place through the court of Ezra the Scribe, which comprised one hundred and twenty elders who were called 'the Men of the Great Assembly' (Anshei Knesset Ha-gedola). The Sages said that Ezra the Scribe was one of the last prophets, and that his prophetic name was Malakhi (Megilla 15a), and together with the Men of the Great Assembly and the people he asked God to remove from them the evil inclination for idolatry. As it is stated: "And Ezra blessed the Lord, the great God" (with the Explicit Name), "and they cried out with a loud voice to the Lord their God" (Neḥemya 8:6; 9:4). The Sages described (Yoma 69b) what happened then by way of parable and image: they cried out with a loud voice about the evil inclination for idolatry, on account of which the Temple had been destroyed, the righteous had been killed and Israel had been exiled from its land, and it was still dancing among them to make them sin. They said to God: You gave us the evil inclination in order to increase our reward when we overcome it; since we do not succeed in standing against it, we want neither it nor its reward. A note fell from heaven on which was written 'Truth'. They understood that their request had been accepted. They sat in fasting for three days and three nights, and something like a young fiery lion came out of the Holy of Holies. The prophet said to Israel: This is the evil inclination. When they seized it, a hair came loose from it, and it raised its voice in a roar, and its voice travelled four hundred parasangs. The sages feared that perhaps Heaven would have mercy on it. A prophet said to them: Throw it into a lead pot and cover it, for lead absorbs sound, as it is stated (Zekharya 5:8): "And he said: This is wickedness; and he cast it into the midst of the ephah, and he cast the lead weight upon its mouth." Thus on the one hand they prevented its strong influence, and on the other hand they did not abolish it by killing it.

After the destruction of the Second Temple, even the manifestation of the holy spirit (ruaḥ ha-kodesh) that inspired the Sages weakened, and in parallel the influence of idols and sorcery steadily decreased (see above 16:4, 18).14

sections.title: Sorcery in Our Times
sections.html:
The weakening of the power of pagan cults and of powerful sorcery gave room to the sages of Israel to clarify the foundations of faith and of the Torah and to determine precisely the details of the mitzvot and their fine points. For even after prophecy ceased, and the holy spirit no longer appeared openly as at first, divine inspiration did not cease from the sages of Israel. And even in exile, the holy spirit rested upon their study, helping them to arrive at the truth of the Torah and to advance the world secretly toward its repair (above 17:7). Thus, gradually, the light of faith in God's unity began to spread in the world.

In parallel to this, throughout all the generations people continued to be drawn after sorcerers. Indeed, unlike in the past, sorcerers no longer occupied a central place in society, but on the margins people told in whispers of their power to know the future and to bring about changes beyond nature, and simple folk as well as princes and counts turned to them in times of trouble, so that they would curse their enemies and remove obstacles from their path. In doing so they agreed to give up their faith in the responsibility placed on man to repair himself and the world, and sold their souls to sorcerers who, with the help of forces of impurity, tried to help them defeat their enemies and increase their status and wealth.

But the more the Torah was studied and clarified by the sages of Israel, the more the light of wisdom was revealed in the world, and the desire to make use of sorcerers decreased. And even among the sorcerers there were some who became less evil, and some of them even refrained from engaging in curses and sought to use their power to do good.

And the more Israel continued to cleave to the Torah and the mitzvot, despite all the sufferings and terrible trials, the more the world was repaired, until the hour arrived and the light of salvation began to sparkle, and Israel began to return to its land, and the light of prophecy is beginning gradually to return to rest upon the world. As it is stated (Yoel 3:1): "And it shall come to pass afterward that I will pour out My spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, your old men shall dream dreams, your young men shall see visions."

In parallel, the inclination to develop spiritual powers, emotion and imagination is also growing stronger, and those drawn after kinds of sorcery are multiplying; these are indeed not as harsh and evil as in the past, but they still greatly interfere with receiving the clear light of God, which is the foundation of prophecy. We must strengthen ourselves in the mitzvot of the Torah, and beware of being tempted after the deceptive spirituality of various guides who claim to bring success and health with the aid of sorcery and fortune-telling by mystical means, and thereby lead a person astray from the straight path. Instead, we must strengthen ourselves in the faith that everything that happens to us is from God, and to Him alone we will turn in prayer, and only according to His Torah will we examine our ways and refine our character traits; and through this we will merit true blessing and a good life, and prophecy will return to shine in all its splendour.
